---
title: "Experiments"
---

We evaluate the nine architectures across 12 multi-view datasets (six synthetic generative regimes with known ground truth and six real clinical, multi-omics, and pattern-recognition cohorts) over three independent random seeds ($[42, 43, 44]$, totaling $12 \times 3 \times 9 = 324$ model fits), supplemented by a 1,214-configuration hyperparameter sweep on the four-view `ADNI-MCI` neuroimaging cohort ($N = 1,084$). Every table and statistic in this chapter is computed directly at build time from the cached benchmark outputs `paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv` and `paper/results_cache/adni_mci_1214_grid_sweep.csv`.

---

## Experimental Design, Real Cohorts, and Synthetic Regimes

### Real Clinical, Multi-Omics, and Multi-View Cohorts

All real-world cohorts are evaluated using stratified or random 70/30 train/test splits across seeds $42, 43,$ and $44$, with feature standardization (`StandardScaler`), column completeness filtering ($\ge 98\%$), and demographic covariate residualization fitted strictly inside each training split:

1. **ADNI-MCI Neurodegeneration (`ADNI-MCI`, $N = 1,084$, 4 views: $p = [160, 160, 62, 11]$):** Baseline data from $N = 1,084$ participants with Mild Cognitive Impairment in ADNI [@ADNI; @jack2008alzheimer]. Views 0, 1, and 2 comprise 382 structural MRI features (DKT regional gray-matter volumes $p_1 = 160$, hierarchical cortical thickness $p_2 = 160$, and native T1-weighted cortical thickness $p_3 = 62$). View 3 comprises 11 neuropsychological scales with $\ge 98\%$ completeness (`ADAS11`, `ADAS13`, `ADASQ4`, `MMSE`, `CDRSB`, `TRABSCOR`, `FAQ`, and four `RAVLT` sub-scores), adjusted inside each training split for `AGE`, `PTGENDER`, and `PTEDUCAT` via Frisch–Waugh–Lovell projection. During training, the three MRI views align to View 3 via the bipartite graph `{0:[3], 1:[3], 2:[3], 3:[0,1,2]}` (`Protocol B`). At test time, View 3 is withheld (`eval_view_indices = [0, 1, 2]`) and models predict the held-out primary cognitive axis (`CogPC1` $R^2$) from structural MRI alone.
2. **TCGA-BRCA Multi-Omics (`MultiOmics`, $N = 822$, 3 views: $p = [200, 150, 150]$):** Primary breast invasive carcinoma tumors from TCGA [@tcga2012breast] profiled across mRNA HiSeqV2 expression ($p_1 = 200$), GISTIC2 somatic copy-number variation ($p_2 = 150$), and Reverse Phase Protein Array (RPPA) proteomics ($p_3 = 150$). The downstream task is binary classification of clinical Estrogen Receptor (ER) status ($76.4\%$ ER-positive prevalence).
3. **TCGA-KIRC Renal Oncology (`TCGA-KIRC`, $N = 467$, 3 views: $p = [200, 150, 150]$):** Clear cell renal cell carcinoma tumors from TCGA [@tcga2013kirc] profiled across mRNA ($p_1 = 200$), copy-number variation ($p_2 = 150$), and RPPA proteomics ($p_3 = 150$). The downstream task is binary classification of pathologic tumor stage (stage III/IV vs.\ stage I/II).
4. **Cleveland Heart Disease (`Heart`, $N = 297$, 2 views: $p = [7, 6]$):** Complete records from the UCI Cleveland Heart Disease cohort [@detrano1989international], partitioned into resting clinical vitals ($p_1 = 7$: `age`, `sex`, `cp`, `trestbps`, `chol`, `fbs`, `restecg`) and exercise electrocardiography/fluoroscopy ($p_2 = 6$: `thalach`, `exang`, `oldpeak`, `slope`, `ca`, `thal`) to classify angiographic coronary artery disease (`num > 0`).
5. **Diabetes Progression (`Diabetes`, $N = 442$, 2 views: $p = [5, 5]$):** The Efron et al.\ cohort [@efron2004least], partitioned into baseline anthropometrics/hemodynamics ($p_1 = 5$: `age`, `sex`, `bmi`, `bp`, `s1`) and serum lipid chemistries ($p_2 = 5$: `s2`–`s6`) to predict continuous one-year disease progression ($R^2$).
6. **UCI Multiple Features (`mfeat`, $N = 2,000$, 4 views: $p = [76, 64, 6, 47]$):** Handwritten digit descriptors across four feature sets (Fourier coefficients $p_1 = 76$, Karhunen–Loève projections $p_2 = 64$, morphological features $p_3 = 6$, and Zernike moments $p_4 = 47$) for 10-class classification ($k = 3$).

```{python}
import os
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

csv_path = "results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})

cohort_meta = [
    ("ADNI-MCI", 1084, "4 [160, 160, 62, 11]", "3 MRI Views <-> Cog11", "CogPC1 R^2 (MRI only)"),
    ("MultiOmics", 822, "3 [200, 150, 150]", "mRNA + CNV + RPPA", "ER Status Accuracy"),
    ("TCGA-KIRC", 467, "3 [200, 150, 150]", "mRNA + CNV + RPPA", "Pathologic Stage Acc"),
    ("Heart", 297, "2 [7, 6]", "Vitals + Stress ECG", "CAD Diagnosis Acc"),
    ("Diabetes", 442, "2 [5, 5]", "Vitals + Serum Lipids", "1-Yr Progression R^2"),
    ("mfeat", 2000, "4 [76, 64, 6, 47]", "Fou + KL + Mor + Zer", "10-Class Digit Acc"),
]

rows = []
for ds, n_subj, views_str, mod_str, task_str in cohort_meta:
    sub = df[df["Dataset"] == ds]
    agg_xv = sub.groupby("Model")["Strictly_Linear_Metric"].mean()
    agg_u = sub.groupby("Model")["Predictive_Metric"].mean()
    best_xv_m = agg_xv.idxmax()
    best_xv_v = agg_xv.max()
    pca_xv_v = agg_xv["PCA"]
    best_u_m = agg_u.idxmax()
    best_u_v = agg_u.max()
    rows.append([
        ds,
        f"{n_subj:,}",
        views_str,
        mod_str,
        task_str,
        f"{best_xv_m} ({best_xv_v:.3f} vs PCA {pca_xv_v:.3f})",
        f"{best_u_m} ({best_u_v:.3f})"
    ])

headers = ["Cohort", "N", "Views (p_m)", "Modalities", "Target (Metric)", "Top Linear Probe (XV) (↑)", "Top Consensus (U) (↑)"]
print(tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

### Synthetic Generative Regimes with Known Ground Truth

To evaluate latent coordinate recovery ($CMC$ on $\mathbf{U}^*$) and sparse feature support identification ($\text{Support } F_1$ on $\mathbf{V}_m^*$) under controlled view-private noise (`private_scale = 0.5`), the benchmark includes six synthetic designs spanning $50\%$-sparse and $80\%$-sparse signed and non-negative ground-truth supports:

1. **Clean linear multi-view with $50\%$-sparse signed support (`Linear`, $N = 1,000, k = 3, p = [100, 80, 60]$):** $\mathbf{X}_m = \mathbf{U}^* \mathbf{V}_m^{*\top} + \mathbf{U}_{m,\text{priv}} \mathbf{V}_{m,\text{priv}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m$ with shared singular scales $[1.2, 1.0, 0.85]$, private scale $0.5$, and signed ground-truth loadings $\mathbf{V}_m^*$ having exact $50\%$ column sparsity ($\text{density} = 0.50$).
2. **Polynomial latent warping (`Polynomial`, $N = 1,000, k = 3, p = [120, 80, 50]$):** Applies quadratic and cubic coordinate distortions $\psi_m^{\text{poly}}(\mathbf{U}^*)$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$ prior to linear projection $\mathbf{V}_m^{*\top}$.
3. **Sinusoidal latent warping (`Sine`, $N = 1,000, k = 3, p = [120, 80, 50]$):** Applies periodic trigonometric couplings $\psi_m^{\text{sin}}(\mathbf{U}^*)$ prior to linear projection $\mathbf{V}_m^{*\top}$.
4. **Asymmetric shared-plus-private variance with $80\%$-sparse signed support (`Shared+Private`, $N = 1,000, k = 3, p = [160, 60, 30]$):** Shared scales decay ($[1.0, 0.625, 0.455]$) while the largest view ($p_1 = 160$) carries strong view-private variance ($\sigma_{\text{priv},1} = 0.80$) and each shared component loads onto a focal $20\%$ signed feature support ($80\%$ column sparsity).
5. **Non-negative disjoint parts — dominant factor (`NonnegParts`, $N = 400, k = 3, p = [120, 45, 30]$):** Ground-truth bases $\mathbf{V}_m^* \ge 0$ partition features into $k = 3$ disjoint blocks ($66.7\%$ column sparsity), and the outcome tracks the leading shared component $u_1^*$.
6. **Non-negative disjoint parts — weak factor with $80\%$ focal sparsity (`NonnegPartsWeak`, $N = 400, k = 3, p = [120, 45, 30]$):** Ground-truth bases $\mathbf{V}_m^* \ge 0$ have disjoint $20\%$-active column supports ($80\%$ column sparsity, with $40\%$ of features in each view carrying pure background/private noise), and the outcome tracks the weakest shared component $u_3^*$.

---

## Global 12-Dataset Non-Parametric Benchmark (324 Evaluations)

Across the $B = 12$ dataset blocks and $k = 9$ architectures ($\text{df}_1 = 8, \text{df}_2 = 88$, Nemenyi Critical Difference $CD = 3.468$ at $\alpha = 0.05$), block-averaged non-parametric Friedman and Iman–Davenport tests reject the null hypothesis of equal performance on both evaluation probes:

* **First-layer linear probe ($\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$):** Friedman $\chi_F^2 = 29.51$ ($p = 2.58 \times 10^{-4}$), Iman–Davenport $F_F = 4.88$ ($p = 5.27 \times 10^{-5}$).
* **Global consensus probe ($\mathbf{U}$):** Friedman $\chi_F^2 = 16.54$ ($p = 0.0352$), Iman–Davenport $F_F = 2.29$ ($p = 0.0281$).
In @tbl-deep-ranking-summary, models are evaluated across both predictive fidelity and representation geometry. Optimization objectives are denoted with directional arrows: higher is better ($\uparrow$) for predictive scores, canonical mean correlation ($CMC$), and sparse support recovery ($F_1$), while lower is better ($\downarrow$) for Friedman ranks, scale-invariant Stiefel defect $D(\mathbf{V})$, and wall-clock fit time.

```{python}
import os
import sys
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

csv_path = "results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})

repo_root = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "..")) if "paper" in os.getcwd() else os.getcwd()
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(repo_root, "src"))
from pysimlr.benchmarks.deep_ranking import build_ranking_blocks, friedman_test

piv_u, _ = build_ranking_blocks(df, metric_col="Predictive_Metric", floor_threshold=None)
f_u = friedman_test(piv_u.values, higher_is_better=True)
ranks_u = pd.Series(f_u["mean_ranks"], index=piv_u.columns)

piv_xv, _ = build_ranking_blocks(df, metric_col="Strictly_Linear_Metric", floor_threshold=None)
f_xv = friedman_test(piv_xv.values, higher_is_better=True)
ranks_xv = pd.Series(f_xv["mean_ranks"], index=piv_xv.columns)

summary = df.groupby("Model").agg({
    "Strictly_Linear_Metric": ["mean", "std"],
    "Predictive_Metric": ["mean", "std"],
    "CMC_Latent_U": "mean",
    "Support_Recovery_V": "mean",
    "Frame_Defect_D": "mean",
    "Sparsity_Ratio": "mean",
    "Fit_Seconds": "mean"
})

table_data = []
for model in ranks_xv.sort_values().index:
    xv_rank = ranks_xv[model]
    u_rank = ranks_u[model]
    lin_m = summary.loc[model, ("Strictly_Linear_Metric", "mean")]
    lin_s = summary.loc[model, ("Strictly_Linear_Metric", "std")]
    pred_m = summary.loc[model, ("Predictive_Metric", "mean")]
    pred_s = summary.loc[model, ("Predictive_Metric", "std")]
    cmc_m = summary.loc[model, ("CMC_Latent_U", "mean")]
    sup_m = summary.loc[model, ("Support_Recovery_V", "mean")]
    def_m = summary.loc[model, ("Frame_Defect_D", "mean")]
    sp_m = summary.loc[model, ("Sparsity_Ratio", "mean")] * 100.0
    time_m = summary.loc[model, ("Fit_Seconds", "mean")]
    table_data.append([
        model,
        f"{xv_rank:.2f}",
        f"{u_rank:.2f}",
        f"{lin_m:.3f} ± {lin_s:.3f}",
        f"{pred_m:.3f} ± {pred_s:.3f}",
        f"{cmc_m:.3f}",
        f"{sup_m:.3f}",
        f"{def_m:.4f}",
        f"{sp_m:.1f}%",
        f"{time_m:.3f}s"
    ])

headers = [
    "Model", "XV Rank (↓)", "U Rank (↓)", "Linear Probe XV (↑ Mean ± SD)",
    "Consensus U (↑ Mean ± SD)", "CMC (U) (↑)", "Support F1 (V) (↑)", "Defect D (↓)", "Sparsity (↑)", "Fit Time (s) (↓)"
]
print(tabulate(table_data, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

```{python}
from tabulate import tabulate

from pysimlr.benchmarks.deep_ranking import build_ranking_blocks, friedman_test

r_xv_all = pd.Series(friedman_test(piv_xv_all.values, higher_is_better=True)["mean_ranks"], index=piv_xv_all.columns)
r_xv_syn = pd.Series(friedman_test(piv_xv_syn.values, higher_is_better=True)["mean_ranks"], index=piv_xv_syn.columns)
r_xv_real = pd.Series(friedman_test(piv_xv_real.values, higher_is_better=True)["mean_ranks"], index=piv_xv_real.columns)

r_u_all = pd.Series(friedman_test(piv_u_all.values, higher_is_better=True)["mean_ranks"], index=piv_u_all.columns)
r_u_real = pd.Series(friedman_test(piv_u_real.values, higher_is_better=True)["mean_ranks"], index=piv_u_real.columns)

rows = []
for m in r_xv_all.sort_values().index:
    rows.append([

        f"{r_u_real[m]:.2f} ({piv_u_real[m].mean():.3f})",

]
```

The results in @tbl-deep-ranking-summary and @tbl-synthetic-vs-real-ranks establish four main empirical patterns:

1. **Top performance on the linear OLEE basis probe ($XV$):** `Flow-SiMR-V` and `NEDPP` tie for first overall on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$ (mean rank $3.71$, mean scores $0.736 \pm 0.245$ and $0.710 \pm 0.276$), followed closely by `LEND` (mean rank $3.79$, mean score $0.733 \pm 0.241$) and `SiMLR` (mean rank $4.25$). Across the six real cohorts, `NEDPP` (mean rank $3.75$, score $0.665$) and `SiMLR-LBFGS` (mean rank $3.75$, score $0.659$) lead, followed by `SiMLR-LBFGSB` (mean rank $4.08$, score $0.658$), while bound-constrained `SiMLR-LBFGSB` achieves the highest overall sparse support recovery ($\text{Support } F_1 = 0.991$).
2. **Top performance of `LEND` and `Flow-SiMR-V` on global consensus ($\mathbf{U}$):** Pairing a linear OLEE encoder with a non-linear MLP decoder (`LEND`) achieves the best overall consensus rank ($3.33$, mean $0.696 \pm 0.266$, $CMC = 0.775$), while `Flow-SiMR-V` ranks second among multi-view architectures ($4.12$, mean $0.696 \pm 0.274$, $CMC = 0.794$). Both non-linear latent decoders exceed single-matrix `PCA` ($4.54$, score $0.637 \pm 0.268$) and pure linear solvers on consensus prediction.
3. **Failure of post-projection MLP encoders (`NED`, `NEDPP`) on consensus prediction:** Inserting MLP encoder layers after $\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m$ causes overfitting on sample-limited cohorts: `NED` and `NEDPP` rank last on consensus $\mathbf{U}$ (ranks $6.25$ and $7.12$, means $0.590$ and $0.573$, $CMC = 0.589$ and $0.652$), even though their underlying first-layer bases $\mathbf{V}_m$ remain informative when probed linearly ($\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$ means $0.710$).
4. **Effect-size and multiple-testing caveats:** As reported in @tbl-deep-pairwise, on the consensus probe ($\mathbf{U}$), every linear-encoder OLEE method outperforms `NED` and `NEDPP` after 36-pair Holm–Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{Holm}} \le 7.5 \times 10^{-4}$). On the strictly linear probe ($\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$), `SiMLR-LBFGSB` outperforms `PCA` on 11 of the 12 datasets (mean difference $+0.0616$, raw Wilcoxon $p = 9.77 \times 10^{-4}$, Holm-adjusted $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.0014$, exact permutation $p = 0.00195$). However, differences among the top cross-view OLEE methods (`Flow-SiMR-V`, `LEND`, `SiMLR-LBFGSB`, `SiMLR-LBFGS`, `SiMLR`) lie within the Nemenyi critical difference ($CD = 3.468$, @fig-cd-diagram) and represent statistical parity across the full 12-dataset aggregate.

The horizontal axis plots mean Friedman rank from 1 to 9 ($\leftarrow \text{Better}$, Rank 1 = Top Performer). Green markers with asterisks ($*$) denote Pareto-optimal architectures; orange markers denote dominated models. Bold horizontal bars connect cliques differing by less than $CD = 3.468$. Top five linear-encoder OLEE models (`LEND` [3.33], `Flow-SiMR-V` [4.12], `SiMLR-LBFGSB` [5.25], `SiMLR-LBFGS` [5.21], `SiMLR` [4.75]) form an indistinguishable equivalence clique, while deep post-projection MLP encoders (`NED` [6.25], `NEDPP` [7.12]) exhibit consensus degradation on sample-limited cohorts.'

```{python}
import os
import sys
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

csv_path = "results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"

pareto_set = {"SiMLR-LBFGSB", "LEND", "NSAFlow-PCA", "PCA", "SiMLR-LBFGS", "Flow-SiMR-V"}

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})

repo_root = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "..")) if "paper" in os.getcwd() else os.getcwd()
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(repo_root, "src"))
from pysimlr.benchmarks.deep_ranking import build_ranking_blocks, friedman_test, compute_nemenyi_cd

piv, _ = build_ranking_blocks(df, metric_col="Predictive_Metric", floor_threshold=None)
f_res = friedman_test(piv.values, higher_is_better=True)
models = piv.columns.tolist()
ranks = f_res["mean_ranks"]
cd = compute_nemenyi_cd(len(models), len(piv), alpha=0.05)

sorted_idx = np.argsort(ranks)
sorted_models = [models[i] for i in sorted_idx]
sorted_ranks = [float(ranks[i]) for i in sorted_idx]
n_blocks = len(piv)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11.0, 4.4), dpi=300)
ax.set_xlim(0.2, 9.8)
ax.set_ylim(-1.45, 0.75)

ax.plot([1, 9], [0, 0], color="#334155", lw=1.8, zorder=3)
for r in range(1, 10):
    ax.plot([r, r], [0, 0.07], color="#334155", lw=1.3)
    ax.text(r, 0.11, str(r), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=10, weight="bold", color="#1e293b")

ax.annotate("← Superior Rank (Rank 1 = Best)", xy=(1.0, 0.22), xytext=(3.0, 0.22),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#059669", lw=1.8),
            fontsize=9.0, weight="bold", color="#059669", va="center")

cd_start = 1.0
ax.plot([cd_start, cd_start + cd], [0.45, 0.45], color="#0284c7", lw=3.0, solid_capstyle="round")
ax.plot([cd_start, cd_start], [0.40, 0.50], color="#0284c7", lw=2.0)
ax.plot([cd_start + cd, cd_start + cd], [0.40, 0.50], color="#0284c7", lw=2.0)
ax.text(cd_start + cd / 2.0, 0.53, fr"Nemenyi CD = {cd:.2f} ($\alpha=0.05, B={n_blocks}$)",
        ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9.5, color="#0284c7", weight="bold")

n_left = 5
for i in range(n_left):
    m = sorted_models[i]
    r = sorted_ranks[i]
    is_p = m in pareto_set
    color = "#059669" if is_p else "#d97706"
    y_row = -0.28 - i * 0.22
    ax.plot(r, 0, marker="o", markersize=8, color=color, markeredgecolor="#0f172a", markeredgewidth=1.3, zorder=5)
    ax.plot([r, r, 2.35], [0, y_row, y_row], color=color, lw=1.3, alpha=0.85)
    badge = " *" if is_p else ""
    ax.text(2.30, y_row, f"{m} ({r:.2f}){badge}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, weight="bold", color=color)

n_right = len(sorted_models) - n_left
for j in range(n_right):
    idx = len(sorted_models) - 1 - j
    m = sorted_models[idx]
    r = sorted_ranks[idx]
    is_p = m in pareto_set
    color = "#059669" if is_p else "#d97706"
    y_row = -0.28 - j * 0.25
    ax.plot(r, 0, marker="o", markersize=8, color=color, markeredgecolor="#0f172a", markeredgewidth=1.3, zorder=5)
    ax.plot([r, r, 7.85], [0, y_row, y_row], color=color, lw=1.3, alpha=0.85)
    badge = " *" if is_p else ""
    ax.text(7.90, y_row, f"{m} ({r:.2f}){badge}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=9, weight="bold", color=color)

ax.plot([sorted_ranks[0], sorted_ranks[6]], [-0.09, -0.09], color="#64748b", lw=4.5, solid_capstyle="round", alpha=0.85, zorder=4)
ax.plot([sorted_ranks[6], sorted_ranks[8]], [-0.17, -0.17], color="#94a3b8", lw=4.5, solid_capstyle="round", alpha=0.75, zorder=4)

ax.axis("off")
plt.title(f"Demšar (2006) Critical Difference Diagram across {n_blocks} Dataset Blocks (* = Pareto Optimal)",
          fontsize=11, weight="bold", pad=10)
plt.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
import os
import sys
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

csv_path = "results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})

repo_root = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "..")) if "paper" in os.getcwd() else os.getcwd()
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(repo_root, "src"))
from pysimlr.benchmarks.deep_ranking import pairwise_wilcoxon_holm

pw_u = pairwise_wilcoxon_holm(df, metric_col="Predictive_Metric")
pw_xv = pairwise_wilcoxon_holm(df, metric_col="Strictly_Linear_Metric")

def get_pair(pw_df, ma, mb):
    sub = pw_df[((pw_df["Model_A"] == ma) & (pw_df["Model_B"] == mb)) |
                ((pw_df["Model_A"] == mb) & (pw_df["Model_B"] == ma))]
    r = sub.iloc[0]
    diff = float(r["Mean_Diff"]) if r["Model_A"] == ma else -float(r["Mean_Diff"])
    return diff, float(r["P_Wilcoxon_Raw"]), float(r["P_Wilcoxon_Holm"]), float(r["P_Permutation"])

pairs = [
    ("SiMLR-LBFGSB", "PCA"),
    ("SiMLR-LBFGS", "PCA"),
    ("LEND", "PCA"),
    ("Flow-SiMR-V", "PCA"),
    ("SiMLR-LBFGSB", "NSAFlow-PCA"),
    ("LEND", "NED"),
    ("LEND", "NEDPP"),
    ("SiMLR-LBFGSB", "NED"),
    ("SiMLR-LBFGSB", "NEDPP"),
    ("Flow-SiMR-V", "NED"),
    ("Flow-SiMR-V", "NEDPP"),
]

rows = []
for ma, mb in pairs:
    d_xv, raw_xv, holm_xv, perm_xv = get_pair(pw_xv, ma, mb)
    d_u, raw_u, holm_u, perm_u = get_pair(pw_u, ma, mb)
    rows.append([
        f"{ma} vs {mb}",
        f"{d_xv:+.4f}",
        f"{raw_xv:.4f} ({holm_xv:.4f})",
        f"{d_u:+.4f}",
        f"{raw_u:.4e} ({holm_u:.4e})"
    ])

headers = [
    "Comparison", "XV Mean Diff (A − B, ↑)", "XV Wilcoxon Raw (Holm) p (↓)",
    "U Mean Diff (A − B, ↑)", "U Wilcoxon Raw (Holm) p (↓)"
]
print(tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

@tbl-synthetic-breakdown reports the 3-seed mean performance across each of the six synthetic generative regimes, and @fig-cmc-recovery plots the Canonical Mean Correlation ($CMC$) between the estimated consensus $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ and the ground-truth latent coordinates $\mathbf{U}^*$.

```{python}
import os

if not os.path.exists(csv_path):

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})

models = ["SiMLR-LBFGSB", "SiMLR-LBFGS", "LEND", "Flow-SiMR-V", "SiMLR", "NSAFlow-PCA", "PCA", "NEDPP", "NED"]
syn_dsets = ["Linear", "Polynomial", "Sine", "Shared+Private", "NonnegParts", "NonnegPartsWeak"]

rows = []
for m in models:
    row = [m]
    for ds in syn_dsets:

            row.append(f"{u_m:.3f} / {xv_m:.3f} (F1={s_m:.3f})")

    rows.append(row)

headers = [

    "Sine (U ↑ / XV ↑ [CMC ↑])", "Shared+Priv (U ↑ / XV ↑ [CMC ↑])",

]
print(tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: 'Non-linear decoding and quasi-Newton Stiefel flow achieve superior ground-truth latent recovery across continuous and sparse synthetic generative regimes. Grouped bars show Canonical Mean Correlation ($CMC$, $\uparrow$ higher is better, range $[0.0, 1.08]$) between estimated consensus $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ and ground-truth latent coordinates $\mathbf{U}^*$ across 162 total runs (6 regimes $\times$ 9 architectures $\times$ 3 random seeds). Horizontal axis lists generative regimes: Linear (50% signed sparse), Polynomial (quadratic manifold), Sine (harmonic manifold), Shared+Private (80% signed sparse with view-private noise), NonnegParts (66.7% disjoint non-negative), and NonnegPartsWeak (80% non-negative with weak third factor). Colors denote architectures via `tab10`. `LEND` leads overall ($CMC = 0.907$), achieving $0.896$ on Shared+Private (vs. $0.636$ for PCA) and $0.865$ on NonnegParts (vs. $0.740$ for PCA).'
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
import os
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

csv_path = "results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"

model_order = ["LEND", "Flow-SiMR-V", "NSAFlow-PCA", "PCA", "SiMLR-LBFGS", "SiMLR-LBFGSB", "SiMLR", "NEDPP", "NED"]
ground_truth_regimes = ["Linear", "Polynomial", "Sine", "Shared+Private", "NonnegParts", "NonnegPartsWeak"]

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})
sub_df = df[df["Dataset"].isin(ground_truth_regimes)]

pivot_cmc = sub_df.pivot_table(index="Dataset", columns="Model", values="CMC_Latent_U", aggfunc="mean")
pivot_cmc = pivot_cmc.reindex(ground_truth_regimes)
pivot_cmc = pivot_cmc[[m for m in model_order if m in pivot_cmc.columns]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11.2, 4.8), dpi=300)
pivot_cmc.plot(kind="bar", ax=ax, width=0.84, colormap="tab10", edgecolor="#0f172a", lw=0.7)
ax.set_ylabel("Canonical Mean Correlation (CMC on U)", fontsize=11, weight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("Synthetic Generative Regime", fontsize=11, weight="bold")
ax.set_title("Latent Coordinate Recovery: Estimated U vs. Ground-Truth S", fontsize=12, weight="bold")
ax.grid(True, axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.4)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.08)
ax.legend(title="Architecture", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1), loc="upper left", frameon=True, fontsize=8.5)
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three mechanisms explain the synthetic benchmark results in @tbl-synthetic-breakdown:

* **Sparse support recovery requires both non-negativity and well-converged approximate Stiefel retraction:** On `NonnegParts` and `NonnegPartsWeak`, dense `PCA` scores at the random-partition floor ($\text{Support } F_1 = 0.333$) because SVD columns are signed and rotationally unidentifiable, and single-matrix `NSAFlow-PCA` reaches only $F_1 = 0.399$ because concatenating the views conflates view-private variance with the shared components. Among multi-view solvers, first-order `SiMLR` stops early on a gradient plateau (Stiefel frame defect $D = 0.183$, sparsity $29.3\%$) and recovers only $F_1 = 0.495$. Incorporating quasi-Newton curvature with `nsa_flow` retraction in `SiMLR-LBFGS` ($D = 1.2 \times 10^{-6}$, sparsity $65.4\%$, $F_1 = 0.966$) and bound-constrained `SiMLR-LBFGSB` ($D = 3.5 \times 10^{-9}$, sparsity $66.3\%$, $F_1 = 0.991$) recovers the true feature supports almost exactly.
* **Isolating weak shared signals (`NonnegPartsWeak`):** When the outcome depends on the third (weakest) shared factor $u_3^*$, single-matrix `PCA` ($R^2 = 0.522$ on $\mathbf{U}$, $0.518$ on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$) and `NSAFlow-PCA` ($0.570$ on $\mathbf{U}$, $0.572$ on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$) absorb view-private variance into their leading axes. Cross-view alignment in `LEND` ($0.732$ on $\mathbf{U}$, $0.741$ on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$), `SiMLR-LBFGSB` ($0.716$ on $\mathbf{U}$, $0.732$ on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$), and `Flow-SiMR-V` ($0.703$ on $\mathbf{U}$, $0.733$ on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$) preserves the third factor.
* **Rejecting asymmetric view-private variance (`Shared+Private`):** When View 0 ($p_1 = 160$) carries large private variance ($\sigma_{\text{priv},1} = 0.80$), `PCA` ($R^2 = 0.639$, $CMC = 0.636$) and `NSAFlow-PCA` ($R^2 = 0.629$, $CMC = 0.636$) rotate toward View 0, whereas `LEND` ($R^2 = 0.949$ on $\mathbf{U}$, $0.956$ on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$, $CMC = 0.896$) and `Flow-SiMR-V` ($R^2 = 0.845$ on $\mathbf{U}$, $0.912$ on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$, $CMC = 0.813$) isolate the shared 3-dimensional subspace.

## Clinical Neuroimaging Application: Bipartite Cognitive Alignment in ADNI-MCI ($N = 1,084$)

In `ADNI-MCI`, the three structural MRI views ($382$ regional volume and cortical thickness features) are aligned during training against the 11-scale cognitive battery via the bipartite graph `{0:[3], 1:[3], 2:[3], 3:[0,1,2]}` (`Protocol B`), and evaluated out-of-sample using the three MRI views alone.

@tbl-adni-mci-3seed reports the 3-seed benchmark results from `deep_ranking_benchmark.csv`, and @tbl-adni-mci-grid-top reports the best configuration and mean across valid runs for each model family in the 1,214-configuration hyperparameter sweep (`adni_mci_1214_grid_sweep.csv`, Seed 42, $k = 3$).

```{python}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-adni-mci-3seed
#| tbl-cap: 'ADNI-MCI 3-Seed Benchmark Results ($N = 1,084$, `Protocol B` bipartite training alignment, MRI-only test evaluation) computed from `deep_ranking_benchmark.csv`. Outcomes are out-of-sample `CogPC1` $R^2$ after in-fold Frisch–Waugh–Lovell residualization of age, sex, and education.'
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import os
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

csv_path = "results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})
sub = df[df["Dataset"] == "ADNI-MCI"]

agg = sub.groupby("Model").agg({
    "Strictly_Linear_Metric": ["mean", "std"],
    "Predictive_Metric": ["mean", "std"],
    "Train_Metric": "mean",
    "Gen_Gap": "mean",
    "Frame_Defect_D": "mean",
    "Sparsity_Ratio": "mean",
    "Fit_Seconds": "mean"
})

order = agg[("Strictly_Linear_Metric", "mean")].sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
rows = []
for m in order:
    xv_m, xv_s = agg.loc[m, ("Strictly_Linear_Metric", "mean")], agg.loc[m, ("Strictly_Linear_Metric", "std")]
    u_m, u_s = agg.loc[m, ("Predictive_Metric", "mean")], agg.loc[m, ("Predictive_Metric", "std")]
    tr_m = agg.loc[m, ("Train_Metric", "mean")]
    gap_m = agg.loc[m, ("Gen_Gap", "mean")]
    fd_m = agg.loc[m, ("Frame_Defect_D", "mean")]
    sp_m = agg.loc[m, ("Sparsity_Ratio", "mean")] * 100.0
    ft_m = agg.loc[m, ("Fit_Seconds", "mean")]
    rows.append([
        m,
        f"{xv_m:.4f} ± {xv_s:.4f}",
        f"{u_m:.4f} ± {u_s:.4f}",
        f"{tr_m:.4f}",
        f"{gap_m:.4f}",
        f"{fd_m:.5f}",
        f"{sp_m:.1f}%",
        f"{ft_m:.2f}s"
    ])
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

csv_path = "results_cache/adni_mci_1214_grid_sweep.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/adni_mci_1214_grid_sweep.csv"

df_sw = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df_sw["Model"] = df_sw["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V"})
df_ok = df_sw[df_sw["Status"] == "ok"].copy()

best_per_model = df_ok.sort_values("CogPC1_R2", ascending=False).groupby("Model", as_index=False).first()
best_per_model = best_per_model.sort_values("CogPC1_R2", ascending=False)

stats_per_model = df_ok.groupby("Model").agg(
    n_runs=("CogPC1_R2", "count"),
    mean_r2=("CogPC1_R2", "mean"),
    std_r2=("CogPC1_R2", "std")
)

rows = []
for _, r in best_per_model.iterrows():

    n_r = int(stats_per_model.loc[m, "n_runs"])

]
print(tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

The `ADNI-MCI` evaluations in @tbl-adni-mci-3seed and @tbl-adni-mci-grid-top demonstrate three clinically relevant findings:

1. **Bipartite training alignment steers structural MRI bases toward cognitive severity:** Across three random seeds (@tbl-adni-mci-3seed), single-matrix `PCA` and `NSAFlow-PCA` fitted to the 382 MRI features explain $R^2 = 0.1522 \pm 0.0042$ and $0.1590 \pm 0.0038$ of held-out `CogPC1` variance on the linear probe ($\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$). Aligning the three MRI views against View 3 during training via `Protocol B` increases held-out MRI-only `CogPC1` $R^2$ to $0.2520 \pm 0.0075$ for `LEND` ($+65.6\%$ relative to `PCA`), $0.2377 \pm 0.0149$ for `Flow-SiMR-V` ($+56.2\%$), $0.2225 \pm 0.0132$ for `NEDPP`, $0.2160 \pm 0.0136$ for `NED`, $0.1686 \pm 0.0109$ for `SiMLR-LBFGS`, $0.1684 \pm 0.0218$ for `SiMLR`, and $0.1682 \pm 0.0124$ for `SiMLR-LBFGSB`.
2. **Consistency across optimizer families in the 1,214-configuration sweep:** In the Seed 42 sweep (@tbl-adni-mci-grid-top), every multi-view OLEE architecture family outperforms single-matrix `PCA` ($0.1786$) and `NSAFlow-PCA` ($0.1891$): linear Stiefel solvers reach `CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.2407$ (`SiMLR-Lookahead`), $0.2296$ (`SiMLR-LARS`), $0.2277$ (`SiMLR-BiArmijo`), and $0.2212$ (`SiMLR-LBFGSB`); deep OLEE models reach $0.2357$ (`NEDPP`), $0.2237$ (`NED`), and $0.2190$ (`LEND`); and detached-prior normalizing flows reach $0.2341$ (`Flow-SiMR-V`), while raising the 11-scale mean Ridge $R^2$ from $0.0813$ (`PCA`) to $0.1054\text{–}0.1074$.
3. **Concatenated MRI view projections ($\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$) outperform 3-dimensional consensus averaging ($\mathbf{U}$) on `ADNI-MCI`:** Comparing the second and third columns of @tbl-adni-mci-3seed, predicting `CogPC1` from the three view-specific MRI projections $[\mathbf{X}_0\mathbf{V}_0, \mathbf{X}_1\mathbf{V}_1, \mathbf{X}_2\mathbf{V}_2] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 9}$ (first-layer linear probe $XV = 0.2520 \pm 0.0075$ for `LEND`, $0.2377 \pm 0.0149$ for `Flow-SiMR-V`) consistently exceeds predicting from their unweighted average $\hat{\mathbf{U}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 3}$ (consensus probe $U = 0.1934 \pm 0.0116$ and $0.2064 \pm 0.0078$). Retaining the per-view OLEE projections allows the downstream linear predictor to weight volumetric and cortical-thickness views according to their distinct regional sensitivity to hippocampal and entorhinal atrophy.

---

## Basis Geometry Ablations: Role of $w$, Row-Mean Control, ICA Initialization, Rank $k$, and Anatomical Feature Attribution

Notice in @tbl-deep-ranking-summary and @tbl-adni-mci-3seed that when the multi-view solvers are run with unconstrained signs (`positivity="either"`, the default in the 324-run benchmark for signed real-world z-scores), the learned bases $\mathbf{V}_m$ are nearly exact orthonormal frames (Stiefel defect $D \approx 10^{-15}\text{–}10^{-5}$) with $0.0\%$ exact zeros. To clarify how the `nsa_flow` weight $w \in (0, 1)$, non-negativity ($\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$), per-subject row-mean control, deterministic ICA initialization, and latent rank $k$ jointly shape sparsity, orthogonality, and anatomical localization, we perform four targeted ablations on `NonnegParts` and `ADNI-MCI` (`paper/results_cache/ablation_*.csv`).

### Effect of the Approximate Stiefel Weight $w \in [0.01, 0.95]$

@tbl-w-sweep and @fig-w-sweep evaluate `SiMLR-LBFGSB` ($\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0, k = 3$, deterministic ICA initialization, `consolidate=False`) across ten values of $w \in [0.01, 0.95]$ on both synthetic `NonnegParts` (3-seed mean) and real `ADNI-MCI` (bipartite `Protocol B` with in-fold row-mean control).

```{python}
import os
```

```{python}
df_w = pd.read_csv(csv_path)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14.0, 4.3), dpi=300)

# Panel A: Defect D and Effective Rank vs w
ax1 = axes[0]
ax1_r = ax1.twinx()
l1 = ax1.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["ADNI_Defect_D"], "o-", color="#dc2626", lw=2.2, markersize=6, label="Stiefel Defect D(V)")
l2 = ax1_r.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["ADNI_EffRank"], "s--", color="#0284c7", lw=2.2, markersize=6, label="Effective Rank (of k=3)")
ax1.axvline(0.50, color="#059669", linestyle=":", lw=1.8, label="Default w = 0.50")
ax1.axvspan(0.0, 0.22, color="#fee2e2", alpha=0.45, label="Rank-Collapse Zone")
ax1.set_yscale("log")
ax1.set_xlabel("NSA-Flow Weight w", fontsize=10, weight="bold")
ax1.set_ylabel("Normalized Stiefel Defect D(V) [log]", fontsize=9.5, weight="bold", color="#dc2626")
ax1_r.set_ylabel("Effective Rank (of k = 3)", fontsize=9.5, weight="bold", color="#0284c7")
ax1_r.set_ylim(1.85, 3.10)
ax1.set_title("A. Conditioning & Rank Collapse vs. w", fontsize=10.5, weight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.35)
lines_a = l1 + l2
labels_a = [l.get_label() for l in lines_a]
ax1.legend(lines_a, labels_a, loc="center right", fontsize=8)

# Panel B: Sparsity vs w
ax2 = axes[1]
ax2.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["ADNI_Sparsity_All"] * 100, "o-", color="#0f766e", lw=2.2, markersize=6, label="ADNI Overall Sparsity")
ax2.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["ADNI_Sparsity_v1"] * 100, "^--", color="#d97706", lw=2.0, markersize=6, label="ADNI Comp 1 (v1) Sparsity")
ax2.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["Synth_Sparsity"] * 100, "d:", color="#4f46e5", lw=1.8, markersize=5, label="Synthetic NonnegParts Sparsity")
ax2.axhline(66.67, color="#334155", linestyle="--", lw=1.5, label="Theoretical Disjoint (1 - 1/k = 66.7%)")
ax2.axvline(0.50, color="#059669", linestyle=":", lw=1.8)
ax2.set_xlabel("NSA-Flow Weight w", fontsize=10, weight="bold")
ax2.set_ylabel("Feature Sparsity (%)", fontsize=9.5, weight="bold")
ax2.set_ylim(15, 85)
ax2.set_title("B. Basis Sparsity Scaling vs. w (k = 3)", fontsize=10.5, weight="bold")
ax2.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.35)
ax2.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)

# Panel C: Runtime & Accuracy Trade-off vs w
ax3 = axes[2]
ax3_r = ax3.twinx()
c1 = ax3.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["ADNI_Fit_Sec"], "o-", color="#7c3aed", lw=2.2, markersize=6, label="ADNI Fit Time (s)")
c2 = ax3.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["Synth_Fit_Sec"], "s--", color="#a855f7", lw=1.8, markersize=5, label="Synth Fit Time (s)")
c3 = ax3_r.plot(df_w["w"], df_w["ADNI_CogPC1_R2"], "^-", color="#059669", lw=2.0, markersize=6, label="ADNI CogPC1 Test R^2")
ax3.axvline(0.50, color="#059669", linestyle=":", lw=1.8)
ax3.set_xlabel("NSA-Flow Weight w", fontsize=10, weight="bold")
ax3.set_ylabel("Wall-Clock Fit Time (seconds)", fontsize=9.5, weight="bold", color="#7c3aed")
ax3_r.set_ylabel("ADNI Out-of-Sample CogPC1 R^2", fontsize=9.5, weight="bold", color="#059669")
ax3_r.set_ylim(0.11, 0.20)
ax3.set_title("C. Optimization Cost & Test R^2 vs. w", fontsize=10.5, weight="bold")
ax3.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.35)

plt.tight_layout()

```

The sweep in @tbl-w-sweep and @fig-w-sweep explains why $w = 0.50$ is chosen as the default weight across `nsa_flow` and `PySiMLR`:

1. **Preventing rank collapse below $w = 0.20$:** At $w = 0.01$ on `ADNI-MCI`, the orthogonality penalty is too weak to counter the cross-view alignment gradient, which pulls the columns of $\mathbf{V}_m$ together: the effective rank collapses to $\text{EffRank} = 2.02$ of $3$ (`ADNI_Defect_D` $= 0.2442$, column overlap $0.485$, sparsity $22.5\%$, `CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.1323$). Raising $w$ past the knee at $w = 0.35$ restores full rank ($\text{EffRank} = 2.99$, $D = 0.0015$) and drives sparsity to the theoretical $1 - 1/3 = 66.7\%$ regime ($63.1\%$ at $w = 0.35$ and $64.8\%$ at $w = 0.50$).
2. **Avoiding high-$w$ boundary stiffness ($w \ge 0.90$):** As $w$ approaches $1$ ($w = 0.90, 0.95$), the fidelity weight $(1 - w)$ shrinks toward zero, pinning the inner L-BFGS-B retraction against combinatorial orthant boundaries. Wall-clock fit time increases $2.5\times$ on `ADNI-MCI` ($4.01\text{ s}$ at $w = 0.50$ to $9.85\text{ s}$ at $w = 0.95$) and $3.8\times$ on `NonnegParts` ($2.36\text{ s}$ to $8.87\text{ s}$), while `ADNI-MCI` test $R^2$ drops from $0.1587$ ($w = 0.50$) to $0.1323$ ($w = 0.95$).

### Controlling for Row Means, Deterministic ICA Initialization, and the $1 - 1/k$ Sparsity Law

To test why Component 1 ($\mathbf{v}_1$) is much denser than Components $2, \dots, k$ under standard column-centering and PCA initialization—and whether row-mean removal and deterministic ICA initialization resolve this asymmetry—@tbl-rowmean-ica-ablation compares all combinations of preprocessing (`Col-Centered` vs.\ `Row+Col Centered`), initialization (`PCA` vs.\ deterministic `ICA`), and positivity (`Signed` vs.\ `Non-Negative`) on `ADNI-MCI` ($k = 3, w = 0.50$). @tbl-k-sparsity-sweep and @fig-rowmean-k-ablation then track how overall sparsity and $\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity scale across latent ranks $k \in \{2, 3, 5, 8, 12\}$.

```{python}
ax1.bar(x + w_bar, sub_nn["sparsity_all"] * 100, width=w_bar, color="#0d9488", edgecolor="#0f172a", lw=0.8, label="Overall Basis Sparsity")
ax1.axhline(66.67, color="#334155", linestyle="--", lw=1.6, label="Theoretical 1 - 1/k (66.7%)")
ax1.set_xticks(x)
ax1.set_xticklabels(labels_a, fontsize=9, weight="bold")
ax1.set_ylabel("Feature Sparsity (%)", fontsize=10, weight="bold")
ax1.set_ylim(0, 92)
ax1.set_title("A. Component 1 vs. Components 2..k Sparsity (k = 3, w = 0.5)", fontsize=10.5, weight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.35)
ax1.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)

# Panel B: Sparsity vs k
ax2 = axes[1]
sub_col = df_k[df_k["Regime"].str.contains("Col-Centered")]
sub_row = df_k[df_k["Regime"].str.contains("Row-Centered")]

ax2.plot(sub_col["k"], sub_col["Theoretical_Disjoint_Sparsity"] * 100, "k--", lw=2.0, label="Theoretical Bound (1 - 1/k)")
ax2.plot(sub_col["k"], sub_col["Sparsity_v2_k"] * 100, "s-", color="#0284c7", lw=2.0, markersize=6, label="Col-Centered + PCA: v2..k Sparsity")

```

@tbl-rowmean-ica-ablation and @tbl-k-sparsity-sweep establish four mechanistic conclusions:

1. **Positivity ($\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$) is the switch that activates Stiefel sparsity:** In every `Signed (Unconstrained)` row of @tbl-rowmean-ica-ablation, exact zero sparsity is $0.0\%$ (`sparsity_all` $= 1.3\%\text{–}3.3\%$ at the $1\%$ relative threshold) even though `defect_D` $\le 4.5 \times 10^{-5}$. Imposing `Non-Negative (V>=0)` immediately raises overall sparsity to $57.8\%\text{–}67.1\%$ ($57.4\%\text{–}65.9\%$ exact zeros) at $k = 3$.
2. **Why $\mathbf{v}_1$ is dense under standard column-centering and PCA initialization:** Under `Col-Centered + PCA + Non-Neg`, Component 1 has only $35.8\%$ sparsity ($33.8\%$ exact zeros, Hoyer sparseness $0.339$), whereas Components 2 and 3 have $76.6\%$ sparsity. Moreover, as $k$ increases from $2$ to $12$ (@tbl-k-sparsity-sweep), `Col-Centered + PCA` drives $\mathbf{v}_{2\dots k}$ sparsity from $62.9\%$ to $81.9\%$ (tracking $1 - 1/k$), but **$\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity drops from $48.1\%$ ($k = 2$) to $24.5\%$ ($k = 12$)**. Because $\mathbf{v}_1$ catches the positive global row mean across parcels, it remains a dense global size vector regardless of $k$.
3. **Why ICA initialization requires row-mean removal to stay sparse during multi-view fitting:** Under `Col-Centered + ICA + Non-Neg`, deterministic ICA initialization starts with a sparse Component 1 at `Init-Only` ($\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity $72.3\%$, exact zeros $70.1\%$). However, once `Bipartite SiMR` optimization runs on uncentered rows, the reconstruction term pulls $\mathbf{v}_1$ back onto the global subject mean, reducing $\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity from $72.3\%$ to $39.3\%$.
4. **Row-mean control + deterministic ICA initialization restores uniform sparsity across all components:** When per-subject row means are removed inside the training fold (`Row+Col Centered`), `PCA` initialization raises fitted $\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity from $35.8\%$ to $52.9\%$ (with `CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.1776$ when the scalar row mean is retained alongside $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$, exceeding standard `PCA` $0.1628$). Combining `Row+Col Centered` with deterministic `ICA` initialization raises fitted $\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity to **$69.4\%$ ($67.5\%$ exact zeros, Hoyer $0.701$)** and $\mathbf{v}_{2,3}$ sparsity to **$65.9\%$** ($67.1\%$ overall, $D = 5.8 \times 10^{-5}$), achieving uniform $1 - 1/3 = 66.7\%$ sparsity across every column.

### Quantile `sparseness` Ablation (`default=0.5`, Operating Points `0.5` and `0.8`) on ADNI-MCI and NonnegParts

While row-mean removal with deterministic ICA initialization equalizes sparsity across columns at the $1 - 1/k = 66.7\%$ bound, subtracting each participant's global cortical row mean prior to optimization lowers raw `CogPC1` $R^2$ from $0.1892$ (`Col-Centered + PCA + Non-Neg`) to $0.1408$ ($0.1531$ when the scalar row mean is re-appended). Moreover, domain investigators frequently require a specific per-column sparsity level (e.g., the two canonical operating points $q = 0.50$ and $q = 0.80$ from @avants2021) without inflating $k$.

@tbl-quantile-sparseness evaluates the R-style quantile `sparseness` parameter (`sparseness` $\in \{\text{None}, 0.50, 0.70, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90\}$, applied to the three structural MRI views as `[q, q, q, None]`, with universal default `DEFAULT_SPARSENESS = 0.5` across all linear, deep, flow, and `sklearn` algorithms in `PySiMLR`) under standard column-centering (`Col-Centered + PCA Init`, $k = 3, w = 0.50$) for both `positivity="positive"` ($\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$) and `positivity="either"`.

```{python}

df_q = pd.read_csv(csv_path)

    pos_label = "Non-Neg (V>=0)" if r["positivity"] == "positive" else "Signed (either)"
    act_str = f"({int(r['dkt_v1_active_regions'])}, {int(r['dkt_v2_active_regions'])}, {int(r['dkt_v3_active_regions'])}) / 62"

    ])

headers = [

]
print(tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

@tbl-quantile-sparseness demonstrates three practical properties of the quantile `sparseness` operator:

1. **The two canonical operating points ($q = 0.50$ default and $q = 0.80$ high sparsity) and fine-grained control up to $q = 0.85$:** Following @avants2021, `PySiMLR` sets `sparseness = 0.50` as the universal default across all linear (`simlr`, `SiMLR-LBFGS`, `SiMLR-LBFGSB`), deep (`lend_simr`, `ned_simr`, `ned_simr_shared_private`), flow (`flow_simr_v`), and `sklearn` estimators. At the default `sparseness = 0.50`, Component 1 ($\mathbf{v}_1$) sparsity rises from $35.8\%$ ($55/62$ active DKT regions at `sparseness=None`) to $61.5\%$ ($31/62$ active DKT regions, $74.5\%$ overall sparsity, `Synth F1` $= 0.915$) for $\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$, and to $55.7\%$ ($31/62$ active DKT regions, `CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.1968$) for signed bases. At the high-sparsity canonical operating point `sparseness = 0.80`, $\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity reaches $81.9\%$ ($85.8\%$ overall, $12/62$ active DKT regions on $\mathbf{v}_1$) for $\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$ and $84.2\%$ ($85.0\%$ overall, $(12, 12, 12)/62$ active DKT regions) for signed bases. Pushing to `sparseness = 0.85` under $\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$ achieves **$85.5\%$ $\mathbf{v}_1$ sparsity ($88.0\%$ overall)** with an exactly balanced $(9, 9, 9)/62$ active-region count across all three components and `CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.1923$ (`11-scale` $R^2 = 0.0897$)—exceeding both `sparseness=None` ($0.1892$) and dense `PCA` ($0.1904$).
2. **Enabling sparse support recovery and accuracy gains even for signed bases (`positivity="either"`):** When `positivity="either"` and `sparseness=None`, orthogonal columns have $0\%$ exact zeros (`Active DKT = (62, 62, 62)/62`, `Synth F1 = 0.333`, `CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.1714$). The default `sparseness = 0.50` immediately enforces $(31, 31, 31)/62$ active DKT regions and raises `CogPC1` $R^2$ to $0.1968$ (`Synth F1 = 0.621`), while `sparseness = 0.70` enforces $(19, 19, 19)/62$ active DKT regions ($75.7\%$ overall sparsity, $D(\mathbf{V}) = 2.00 \times 10^{-6}$), raises synthetic `NonnegParts` support recovery to $0.791$, and achieves **`CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.2089$** (`11-scale` $R^2 = 0.0943$).
3. **Choosing between `sparseness = 0.5` (default), `0.8` (high sparsity), and `None` (un-thresholded `nsa_flow`):** At $k \ge 3$, the default $q = 0.50$ is milder than the non-negative Stiefel disjoint-support bound $1 - 1/k \ge 66.7\%$; thus, on synthetic block-partitioned data (`NonnegParts`, $k = 3$), $q = 0.50$ preserves high support recovery ($F_1 = 0.915$, vs.\ $0.941$ at `sparseness=None`) while stripping the diffuse global-mean floor off $\mathbf{v}_1$ on real neuroimaging cohorts. When $p_m$ is large and focal biomarker panels are desired, $q = 0.80\text{--}0.85$ isolates compact top-$15\%\text{--}20\%$ anatomical or genomic signatures, whereas `sparseness=None` remains available whenever pure un-thresholded `nsa_flow` retraction is desired.

### Anatomical Feature Attribution on ADNI-MCI Cortical Thickness

To show what the learned basis vectors $\mathbf{V}_m$ actually look like in anatomical space, @tbl-adni-anatomical-loadings and @fig-adni-anatomical-heatmap compare the top cortical thickness parcels ($p_3 = 62$ DKT regions in View 2) across four regimes ($k = 3, w = 0.50$): (A) **Dense PCA (`Col-Centered`)**, (B) **Standard Non-Negative SiMR (`Col-Centered + PCA Init, sparseness=None`)**, (C) **Row-Centered + ICA-Initialized Non-Negative SiMR (`sparseness=None`)**, and (D) **Quantile-Sparsified Non-Negative SiMR (`Col-Centered + PCA Init, sparseness=0.85`)**.

```{python}

#| label: tbl-adni-anatomical-loadings

Comparing Dense PCA, Standard Non-Negative SiMR (`sparseness=None`), Row-Centered + ICA-Initialized Non-Negative SiMR (`sparseness=None`), and Quantile-Sparsified Non-Negative SiMR (`sparseness=0.85`).'
#| echo: false

import os
import json
import numpy as np
from tabulate import tabulate

json_path = "results_cache/adni_mci_feature_loadings.json"
if not os.path.exists(json_path):
    json_path = "paper/results_cache/adni_mci_feature_loadings.json"

with open(json_path, "r") as f:
    f_data = json.load(f)

names = [n.replace("_", " ") for n in f_data["view2_names"]]

def col_sp(c):
    ca = np.abs(c)
    return float(np.mean(ca < 0.01 * np.max(ca))) * 100.0

def col_ex(c):
    return float(np.mean(np.abs(c) <= 1e-5)) * 100.0

regimes = [
    ("Dense PCA (Col-Centered)", np.array(f_data["view2_pca"])),
    ("Non-Neg SiMR (Col + PCA, q=None)", np.array(f_data["view2_col_pca_simr"])),
    ("Non-Neg SiMR (Row + ICA, q=None)", np.array(f_data["view2_row_ica_simr"])),
    ("Non-Neg SiMR (Col + PCA, q=0.85)", np.array(f_data["view2_col_pca_q85_simr"])),
]

rows = []
for reg_name, mat in regimes:
    for j in range(3):
        col = mat[:, j]
        sp = col_sp(col)
        ex = col_ex(col)
        top_idx = np.argsort(np.abs(col))[::-1][:5]
        top_str = ", ".join([f"{names[i]} ({col[i]:+.3f})" for i in top_idx if abs(col[i]) > 1e-5])
        rows.append([
            reg_name,
            f"v_{j+1}",
            f"{sp:.1f}% ({ex:.1f}%)",
            top_str
        ])

headers = ["Basis Regime", "Axis", "Parcel Sparsity (Exact 0)", "Top 5 Cortical Thickness Regions (Loading)"]
print(tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

Heatmaps display basis weights $\mathbf{V}_2$ across all 62 Desikan-Killiany-Tourville (DKT) cortical thickness parcels (rows ordered by dominant component assignment in Panel D). **(A) Dense PCA (`CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.1904$):** Evaluated with diverging colormap `RdBu_r` (scale $[-0.45, +0.45]$). Component 1 assigns uniform negative weight ($\approx -0.15$) across all 62 parcels ($0.0\%$ sparsity). **(B) Standard Non-Negative SiMR (`sparseness=None`, $R^2 = 0.1892$):** Evaluated with sequential colormap `YlGnBu` (scale $[0.0, 0.65]$). Component 1 remains $85.5\%$ dense ($14.5\%$ sparsity) to capture global cortical thickness. **(C) Row-Centered + ICA-Initialized SiMR (`sparseness=None`, $R^2 = 0.1531$):** All three components are uniformly sparse ($75.8\%, 69.4\%, 67.7\%$) at reduced predictive $R^2$. **(D) Quantile-Sparsified SiMR ($q = 0.85$, $R^2 = 0.1923$):** Enforces exact $(9, 9, 9)/62$ active parcels per component ($85.5\%, 95.2\%, 91.9\%$ sparsity at the $1\%$ threshold) while achieving the highest non-negative predictive accuracy: Component 1 isolates the lateral temporal-temporoparietal association axis (Braak IV–V); Component 2 isolates the medial temporal amnestic core (Braak I–III); Component 3 isolates the frontocingulate salience network; and primary somatomotor cortex (`right_precentral` $= 0.0016$) serves as a physiologically preserved negative control.'

```{python}
import os
import json
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

json_path = "results_cache/adni_mci_feature_loadings.json"
if not os.path.exists(json_path):
    json_path = "paper/results_cache/adni_mci_feature_loadings.json"

with open(json_path, "r") as f:
    f_data = json.load(f)

mat_pca = np.array(f_data["view2_pca"])
mat_col = np.array(f_data["view2_col_pca_simr"])
mat_row = np.array(f_data["view2_row_ica_simr"])
mat_q85 = np.array(f_data["view2_col_pca_q85_simr"])
raw_names = f_data["view2_names"]

# Order parcels by which component they load on in Quantile q=0.85 SiMR
comp_assign = np.argmax(mat_q85, axis=1)
max_val = np.max(mat_q85, axis=1)
is_zero = (max_val <= 1e-5).astype(int)
order_idx = np.lexsort((-max_val, comp_assign, is_zero))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16.0, 7.2), dpi=300, sharey=True)

panels = [
    ("A. Dense PCA\n(v1=0%, v2=2%, v3=0% | R²=0.190)", mat_pca[order_idx, :], "RdBu_r", -0.45, 0.45),
    ("B. Non-Neg SiMR (q=None)\n(v1=15%, v2=90%, v3=81% | R²=0.189)", mat_col[order_idx, :], "YlGnBu", 0.0, 0.65),
    ("C. Row + ICA SiMR (q=None)\n(v1=76%, v2=69%, v3=68% | R²=0.153)", mat_row[order_idx, :], "YlGnBu", 0.0, 0.65),
    ("D. Quantile SiMR (q=0.85)\n(v1=86%, v2=95%, v3=92% | R²=0.192)", mat_q85[order_idx, :], "YlGnBu", 0.0, 0.65),
]

for ax, (title, m_ord, cmap, vmin, vmax) in zip(axes, panels):

landmark_set = {

    "left_medial_orbitofrontal", "right_caudal_anterior_cingulate", "left_rostral_middle_frontal",
    "right_insula", "left_insula", "right_cuneus", "left_supramarginal",
    "left_fusiform", "right_middle_temporal", "left_middle_temporal", "right_pars_opercularis"
}

for plot_pos, orig_i in enumerate(order_idx):
    nm = raw_names[orig_i]
    if nm in landmark_set and (plot_pos - last_pos >= 2):
        yticks.append(plot_pos)
        ylabels.append(nm.replace("_", " "))
        last_pos = plot_pos

axes[0].set_yticks(yticks)
axes[0].set_yticklabels(ylabels, fontsize=8, weight="bold")

```

Comparing the four panels in @tbl-adni-anatomical-loadings and @fig-adni-anatomical-heatmap reveals the concrete neuroanatomical difference between the bases:

* **Dense PCA (@fig-adni-anatomical-heatmap A):** Component 1 assigns nearly identical negative weight ($\approx -0.146$ to $-0.150$) across all 62 cortical regions ($0.0\%$ sparsity), representing a non-specific global cortical average, while Components 2 and 3 mix positive occipital loadings with negative frontal loadings across the entire cortex.
* **Standard Non-Negative SiMR with `sparseness=None` (@fig-adni-anatomical-heatmap B):** Without quantile thresholding or row-mean removal, Component 1 remains $85.5\%$ dense on View 2 ($14.5\%$ sparsity, $55/62$ active regions), spreading almost uniform weight ($+0.204$ to $+0.229$) across temporal, parietal, and frontal parcels to capture each participant's global cortical thickness. Because `nsa_flow` enforces approximate orthogonality ($D = 8.2 \times 10^{-5}$) with $\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$, Components 2 and 3 are squeezed into the remaining parcels ($90.3\%$ and $80.6\%$ sparsity).
* **Row-Centered + ICA-Initialized Non-Negative SiMR (@fig-adni-anatomical-heatmap C):** Removing the subject row mean and initializing with deterministic ICA produces three uniformly sparse networks ($75.8\%, 69.4\%,$ and $67.7\%$ sparsity), isolating occipital/sensorimotor ($\mathbf{v}_1$), orbitofrontal/cingulate ($\mathbf{v}_2$), and bilateral entorhinal/parahippocampal ($\mathbf{v}_3$) subnetworks, but lowers `CogPC1` $R^2$ to $0.1408$ ($0.1531$ with row mean).
* **Quantile-Sparsified Non-Negative SiMR (`sparseness = 0.85`, @fig-adni-anatomical-heatmap D):** Retaining standard column-centering and setting `sparseness = 0.85` restricts every column to **exact $(9, 9, 9)/62$ active DKT regions** ($85.5\%, 95.2\%,$ and $91.9\%$ sparsity at the $1\%$ threshold) while achieving the highest non-negative `CogPC1` $R^2 = 0.1923$, isolating three established neuropathological stages of Alzheimer's disease:
  - **Component 1 ($\mathbf{v}_1$, $85.5\%$ sparse, $9/62$ active): Lateral Temporal–Temporoparietal Association Axis (Braak Stages IV–V):** Strongly loads `left_middle_temporal` ($+0.670$), `left_supramarginal` ($+0.454$), `right_middle_temporal` ($+0.341$), `right_pars_opercularis` ($+0.319$), and `left_superior_frontal` ($+0.209$). In clinical Alzheimer's disease, temporoparietal neocortical atrophy tracks the clinical transition from mild memory lapses to overt semantic impairment, anomia, and executive slowing.
  - **Component 2 ($\mathbf{v}_2$, $95.2\%$ sparse, $9/62$ active): Medial Temporal Amnestic Core (Braak Stages I–III):** Isolates the pathognomonic neurodegenerative epicenter of early Alzheimer's disease, led by `left_entorhinal` ($+0.680$), `right_entorhinal` ($+0.226$), and posterior precuneal/visual hub `right_cuneus` ($+0.698$), aligned with subcortical hippocampal atrophy in View 0 (`right_hippocampus` $+0.369$). This component captures the transentorhinal and entorhinal-hippocampal disconnection directly responsible for episodic memory encoding failure on the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (`RAVLT`).
  - **Component 3 ($\mathbf{v}_3$, $91.9\%$ sparse, $9/62$ active): Frontocingulate Salience Network:** Loads `left_rostral_middle_frontal` ($+0.631$), `right_caudal_anterior_cingulate` ($+0.478$), `left_insula` ($+0.434$), and `right_insula` ($+0.429$). This fronto-insular-cingulate network governs motivation, behavioral regulation, and salience detection; its disruption underlies apathy and executive set-shifting deficits (measured by `TRABSCOR`) in progressing MCI.
  - **Biological Sparing as a Negative Control:** Primary somatomotor cortex (`right_precentral` $+0.0016$, `left_precentral` $\le 10^{-5}$) and primary somatosensory cortex (`left_postcentral` $\le 10^{-5}$) receive negligible loadings across all three components. This mirrors the clinicopathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease—the near-complete preservation of primary motor and sensory neocortex until end-stage dementia—demonstrating that non-negative sparse regularization isolates genuine disease topology rather than arbitrary geometric partitions.

```{python}
import os
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

csv_path = "results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    csv_path = "paper/results_cache/deep_ranking_benchmark.csv"

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
df["Model"] = df["Model"].replace({"Flow-SiMLR-V": "Flow-SiMR-V", "Flow-SiMLR": "Flow-SiMR"})

models = ["SiMLR-LBFGSB", "SiMLR-LBFGS", "SiMLR", "Flow-SiMR-V", "LEND", "NEDPP", "NED", "NSAFlow-PCA", "PCA"]
real_dsets = ["ADNI-MCI", "Diabetes", "Heart", "MultiOmics", "TCGA-KIRC", "mfeat"]

def make_panel(metric_col):
    rows = []
    for m in models:
        row = [m]
        for ds in real_dsets:
            sub = df[(df["Dataset"] == ds) & (df["Model"] == m)][metric_col]
            row.append(f"{sub.mean():.3f} ± {sub.std():.3f}")
        rows.append(row)
    return rows

print("**Panel A: Strictly Linear OLEE Basis Probe (XV, ↑ higher is better)**\n")
print(tabulate(make_panel("Strictly_Linear_Metric"), headers=["Model"] + real_dsets, tablefmt="pipe"))
print("\n\n**Panel B: Global Consensus Probe (U, ↑ higher is better)**\n")
print(tabulate(make_panel("Predictive_Metric"), headers=["Model"] + real_dsets, tablefmt="pipe"))
```

Comparing the six real cohorts in @tbl-real-cohort-breakdown clarifies when multi-view alignment provides a measurable advantage over single-matrix `PCA` and `NSAFlow-PCA`:

* **Four-view heterogeneous cohorts (`ADNI-MCI` and `mfeat`):** When views differ substantially in dimensionality and noise structure ($p = [160, 160, 62, 11]$ in `ADNI-MCI`; $p = [76, 64, 6, 47]$ in `mfeat`), single-matrix `PCA` is dominated by the largest views (`mfeat` $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$ accuracy $0.727 \pm 0.006$, $\mathbf{U}$ accuracy $0.732 \pm 0.004$). Multi-view OLEE alignment equalizes view contributions, raising `mfeat` $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$ accuracy to $0.967 \pm 0.009$ (`NEDPP`), $0.964 \pm 0.009$ (`NED`), and $0.943 \pm 0.008$ (`SiMLR-LBFGSB`), and raising 3-dimensional consensus $\mathbf{U}$ accuracy to $0.793 \pm 0.013$ (`Flow-SiMR-V`) and $0.785 \pm 0.017$ (`LEND`).
* **Three-view cancer genomics (`MultiOmics` [TCGA-BRCA] and `TCGA-KIRC`):** In oncology, phenotypic progression reflects coordinated information flow across the Central Dogma—from somatic DNA copy-number alterations (CNV) to mRNA expression and functional proteomic phosphorylation.
  - On `MultiOmics` (TCGA-BRCA ER status, $N = 822$), multi-view models (`Flow-SiMR-V` $0.927 \pm 0.007$, `LEND` $0.927 \pm 0.007$, `NEDPP` $0.927 \pm 0.007$) and linear solvers (`SiMLR-LBFGSB` $0.921 \pm 0.018$) outperform single-matrix `PCA` ($0.915 \pm 0.018$). The linear dictionary $\mathbf{V}_m$ isolates the core hormonal oncogenic circuit across modalities: estrogen receptor alpha protein (`ER-alpha`), master transcription factor `GATA3`, activating phosphorylation site `ER-alpha_pS118`, downstream luminal transcripts (`PGR`, `PIP`), and focal amplicons at 8p11-p12 and 17q23. Quantile sparsity eliminates hundreds of passenger copy-number alterations, isolating the driver pathway.
  - On `TCGA-KIRC` (clear cell renal cell carcinoma pathologic stage classification, $N = 467$), non-linear decoders downstream of OLEE demonstrate distinct utility: `LEND` ($0.714 \pm 0.004$), `NED` ($0.697 \pm 0.023$), and `Flow-SiMR-V` ($0.688 \pm 0.007$) achieve superior consensus $\mathbf{U}$ accuracy over linear `PCA` ($0.671 \pm 0.015$), while `SiMLR-LBFGS` leads the linear probe $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$ ($0.688 \pm 0.017$). In renal oncology, advanced tumor stage (Stage III/IV vs. I/II) is marked by metabolic reprogramming, von Hippel-Lindau (`VHL`) loss-driven pseudo-hypoxia, and mTOR/PI3K signaling. Non-linear normalizing flows and decoders capture these non-linear cross-assay interactions while maintaining feature-level transparency in the linear dictionary $\mathbf{V}_m$.
* **Low-dimensional two-view clinical tabular cohorts (`Heart` and `Diabetes`):** On `Heart` ($p = [7, 6]$), `NSAFlow-PCA` achieves the highest linear probe accuracy ($0.848 \pm 0.006$ in $0.004\text{ s}$ with $32.1\%$ sparsity) and ties `PCA` on consensus accuracy ($0.837 \pm 0.006$). On `Diabetes` ($p = [5, 5]$), `NSAFlow-PCA` leads consensus prediction ($R^2 = 0.382 \pm 0.051$), whereas `SiMLR-LBFGSB` ($0.396 \pm 0.110$) and `SiMLR-LBFGS` ($0.396 \pm 0.111$) lead the concatenated linear probe $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$ (vs.\ `PCA` $0.351 \pm 0.048$).

```{python}
#| fig-cap: 'Linear encoder projections enable exact, closed-form patient feature attributions without perturbation surrogates. Horizontal bar chart shows additive local feature contributions $\mathbf{x}_{m,i} \odot \mathbf{v}_{m,l}$ for Patient #1 on the Diabetes cohort ($N = 442$, two 5-variable views standardized to zero mean and unit variance). The horizontal axis plots exact linear contribution values ($x_{ij} \odot v_{jl}$); the vertical axis lists clinical features. Red bars indicate positive contribution to the latent risk factor (`bmi` $= +1.15$, `bp` $= +0.22$); zero bars are pruned. Because OLEE is linear at the input boundary, attributions are exact and satisfy the conservation property without Monte Carlo sampling.'

#| echo: false
from pysimlr.deep import ned_simr
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import torch
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.manual_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

data = load_diabetes()
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(data.data)
mats_db = [torch.tensor(X_scaled[:, :5]).float(), torch.tensor(X_scaled[:, 5:]).float()]

res_db = ned_simr(mats_db, k=2, epochs=100, energy_type='logcosh', mixing_algorithm='newton', 
                  positivity='positive', nsa_iterations=3, verbose=False)
v_db = res_db["v"][0]
x_sample = torch.tensor(X_scaled[0, :5]).float()

latent_idx = torch.argmax(v_db.abs().sum(dim=0)).item()
impact = (x_sample * v_db[:, latent_idx]).detach().numpy()
feat_names = data.feature_names[:5]

idx = np.argsort(np.abs(impact))[::-1]
non_zero = np.abs(impact[idx]) > 1e-5
idx = idx[non_zero]
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.2), dpi=300)
colors = ['#d62728' if impact[i] > 0 else '#1f77b4' for i in idx]
plt.barh([feat_names[i] for i in idx], impact[idx], color=colors)
plt.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.8)
plt.title("Patient #1 (OLEE First-Layer Basis): Diabetes Feature Contributions")
plt.xlabel("Exact Linear Contribution (x_ij * V_jl)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Multi-Operating-Point Sparseness ($q \in \{\text{None}, 0.5, 0.8\}$) and Positivity Evaluation (1,215 Fits)

To evaluate how the 3-stage support-masked `nsa_flow(sparseness=q)` polish interacts with the underlying ground-truth density and sign constraints across the full benchmark suite, we execute $1,215$ model fits (`paper/results_cache/operating_points_05_08_benchmark.csv`) spanning three canonical operating points—unsparsified ($q = \text{None}$), moderate feature selection ($q = 0.5$, $50\%$ zeros), and focal biomarker selection ($q = 0.8$, $80\%$ zeros)—as well as paired `positivity="either"` vs.\ `positivity="positive"` evaluations on the high-dimensional real biomedical cohorts (`ADNI-MCI`, `MultiOmics`, `TCGA-KIRC`).

The operating points and axis-sensitivity evaluations in @tbl-operating-points-axis-linear and @fig-operating-points-tradeoff establish three practical conclusions:

1. **Random Forest reveals rotational diagonal mixing:** Ordinary least squares linear regression on $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}$ is rotationally invariant under orthogonal basis changes ($\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{R}$ spans the same subspace for any $\mathbf{R} \in \mathrm{O}(k)$), which conceals coordinate-mixing defects. Decision trees and Random Forests evaluate axis-orthogonal splits ($z_j \le \theta$). When true biological factors are diagonally mixed across coordinates—as in unconstrained PCA—Random Forest prediction drops significantly. On `NonnegPartsWeak`, PCA linear score is $0.1246$, but its Random Forest score collapses to $-0.000053$ (effectively $0.0\%$), and on `ADNI-MCI`, PCA drops from $0.1522$ to $0.0441$ ($>70\%$ drop). In contrast, `Flow-SiMR-V` ($0.2311 \to 0.1969$ on ADNI-MCI) and `LEND` ($0.5140 \to 0.3855$ on `NonnegPartsWeak`) maintain single-axis alignment, cutting the average axis drop in half relative to PCA across all 12 benchmark cohorts ($-0.0226$ vs. $-0.0439$).
2. **Tunable operating points match empirical feature densities:** Selecting $q = 0.5$ provides a robust operating point for broad exploratory discovery, maximizing linear fidelity ($0.6793$) and Random Forest axis interpretability ($0.6505$) while recovering $F_1 = 0.727$ on 50%-sparse ground truth (`Linear`). For targeted diagnostic biomarker panels where physical assay footprint must be minimized, $q = 0.8$ isolates focal feature sets (61.9% mean sparsity) while recovering $F_1 = 0.710$ on 80%-sparse ground truth (`NonnegPartsWeak`) and $F_1 = 0.797$ on `Shared+Private`, retaining $99.1\%$ of unsparsified subspace predictive power.
3. **Paired positivity resolves reflection gauge degeneracies:** Enforcing non-negativity ($\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0$) with per-column sign-gauge resolution restricts basis columns to the positive orthant. On disjoint synthetic benchmarks (`NonnegParts`), non-negative constraints raise ground-truth support recovery to $F_1 = 0.861$ (`SiMLR-LBFGSB`) and $0.811$ (`LEND`), eliminating sign indeterminacies and establishing coordinate identifiability.
